heroText: Cusco is the former Inca capital and Peru's main gateway to the Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu, with steep stone streets, churches and high-altitude plazas. Start at Plaza de Armas, walk up to San Blas, then visit Sacsayhuaman and Qorikancha for the Inca-Spanish layers. Alejandro Velasco Astete airport is close to town, but altitude makes the first day slower.

areas.name: Centro Historico
areas.text: Centro Historico is the easiest first base, with Plaza de Armas, restaurants, museums and tour pickups within short walks.

areas.name: San Blas
areas.text: San Blas is steep, atmospheric and creative, with boutique stays, galleries and views above the main plaza.

areas.name: San Pedro
areas.text: San Pedro is practical for the market, train logistics and budget stays west of the historic core.

areas.name: Wanchaq
areas.text: Wanchaq is flatter and more local, useful for business, longer stays and easier airport-side transfers.
areas.bestFor: longer stays, airport access, local feel

areas.name: Poroy road
areas.text: The Poroy road area is useful only for specific rail or car logistics, not for a classic first Cusco stay.
areas.bestFor: rail logistics, car trips, quiet nights

airports.text: Cusco airport is close to the city, but traffic, altitude and early departures still make transfer timing important.

airportTransfer.note: from Alejandro Velasco Astete International Airport

stayOverview: Centro Historico is the strongest first Cusco base for Plaza de Armas, restaurants and tour pickups. San Blas is scenic but steep, San Pedro is practical and cheaper, Wanchaq helps with airport access, and Poroy only suits rail logistics.
hotelIntro: Cusco hotel choice should account for altitude and hills: Centro Historico is easiest, San Blas is charming but steep, San Pedro is budget-friendly, Wanchaq is practical, and Poroy is mainly for specific train or car plans.
rentalCars: Do not rent a car for Cusco itself; use tours, taxis or drivers for Sacred Valley and highland routes.

travelTips.title: Altitude
travelTips.text: Take the first day slowly, drink water and avoid heavy hiking immediately after arriving at Cusco airport.

travelTips.title: Best base
travelTips.text: Stay near Plaza de Armas for a first visit unless steep streets or late-night noise are a concern.

travelTips.title: Rail timing
travelTips.text: Keep the Cusco plan compact: group nearby sights together and leave enough time for transfers, meals and weather changes.

highlights.title: Plaza de Armas
highlights.text: Plaza de Armas is a named Cusco landmark that helps structure a real visit, adding orientation, local context and a clear route anchor.

highlights.title: Sacsayhuaman
highlights.text: Sacsayhuaman is the monumental Inca site above Cusco, with huge stone walls and broad views over the city.

highlights.title: San Blas
highlights.text: San Blas is Cusco's steep artisan quarter, known for galleries, cafes, guesthouses and views back to the centre.

highlights.title: Qorikancha
highlights.text: Qorikancha shows Cusco's Inca and colonial layers, with Santo Domingo built over the former Temple of the Sun.

highlights.title: San Pedro Market
highlights.text: San Pedro Market is the main food and produce hall, useful for juices, simple meals and local shopping.

highlights.title: Twelve-Angled Stone
highlights.text: The Twelve-Angled Stone is a famous example of Inca masonry on a narrow street near the main plaza.

nearbyIdeas.name: Machu Picchu
nearbyIdeas.label: Heritage
nearbyIdeas.text: Machu Picchu is the essential Cusco-linked trip, requiring advance tickets, train planning and usually a full day or overnight.

nearbyIdeas.name: Sacred Valley
nearbyIdeas.label: Valley
nearbyIdeas.text: The Sacred Valley connects Pisac, Urubamba and Ollantaytambo, often better with one or two nights.

nearbyIdeas.name: Rainbow Mountain
nearbyIdeas.label: Nature
nearbyIdeas.text: Rainbow Mountain is a high-altitude day trip that needs acclimatization, warm layers and realistic fitness expectations.

history.text: Carbon-14 dating of Saksaywaman, the walled complex outside Cusco, established that Killke constructed the fortress about 1100 AD.
Alcaldes were established and regidores on 24 March 1534, which included the brothers Gonzalo Pizarro and Juan Pizarro.
In 1650, a violent earthquake destroyed almost all the colonial-era buildings.
Cusco became the last colonial capital during the rule of Viceroy José de la Serna, who held that position from this city between December 31, 1821, and December 1824.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: According to Inca legend, the city was rebuilt by Sapa Inca Pachacuti, the man who transformed the Kingdom of Cusco from a sleepy city-state into the vast empire of Tawantinsuyu.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: Father Vincente de Valverde became the Bishop of Cusco and built his cathedral facing the plaza.
